288.title: The Catholic Church
288.hook: the largest church, united with the Bishop of Rome, with the Mass at its heart
288.howItsDone: Catholics attend Mass every Sunday and on major feast days, receive communion, and many pray the rosary, go to confession, and honor Mary and the saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Orthodoxy: icons, incense, and iron glowing in the fire. Your line was heaven on earth. What moment of beauty made you forget where you were? Day two hundred eighty-eight.

It's Sunday morning, and the sun is moving around the planet. As it rises over a village in the Philippines, a bell rings and a priest lifts a round white host. An hour or so later, the same thing in Vietnam. Then in India, in Nigeria, in Poland, in Brazil at a packed six o'clock evening Mass, in a little church in Ohio with forty people and a slightly out-of-tune organ. The languages change. The music changes. The words are nearly the same, translated from one Latin book. Somewhere on earth, every hour of every day, someone is celebrating Mass. That's the scale of the church we meet today. It's the largest Christian church on earth: well over a billion people. Today's word is its name.
screen: `THE SUN MOVES AROUND THE WORLD.` → `THE SAME MASS, EVERY HOUR.` → `OVER A BILLION PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The Catholic Church is the communion of churches united with the bishop of Rome, the pope. Catholics trace that role to Peter, and to Jesus's words to him in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." The name Peter means rock. Catholics understand the pope as Peter's successor, a sign and servant of the church's unity. Other Christians read that verse differently, some saying the rock is Peter's faith, or Christ himself. That's one of the oldest conversations in Christian history, and it still goes on. At the heart of Catholic life is the Mass. Catholics believe that in the Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, and they call the Eucharist the source and summit of the Christian life. The word Mass itself comes from the last Latin line of the old service: ite, missa est, go, it is sent. The service ends by sending people out. Around the Mass sit seven sacraments, from baptism to the anointing of the sick, marking a life from birth to death. And here's something many people don't know: the Catholic Church isn't only Roman. Alongside the large Latin church there are more than twenty Eastern Catholic churches, Ukrainian, Maronite, Melkite, Chaldean and others, with their own liturgies, their own customs, some with married priests, all in communion with the pope. And the word catholic itself means universal, from a Greek phrase, according to the whole. We'll come back to that word later on the path.
screen: `UNITED WITH THE BISHOP OF ROME.` · `THE MASS: SOURCE AND SUMMIT.` · `ITE, MISSA EST: GO, IT IS SENT.` · `NOT ONLY ROMAN: EASTERN CATHOLICS.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing a Catholic friend loves. Settle, and breathe. Think of a Catholic you know, or knew: a grandmother, a coworker, a friend from school. What did they love? Maybe the rosary in their pocket. A saint they talked to. Midnight Mass at Christmas. The smell of the church. Hold that one thing in mind with respect. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the Catholic Church. If you don't know any Catholics, picture that little church in Ohio, forty people and an out-of-tune organ. The bell holds the time.
The Catholic Church. The largest Christian church, united with the bishop of Rome, with the Mass at its heart.
Your line: universal. Today, ask a Catholic friend what they love about their church, and just listen. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

289.title: Luther's hammer
289.hook: in 1517 a monk posted 95 theses; he said we're saved by grace through faith
289.howItsDone: Many Protestant churches keep October 31 as Reformation Day, often singing Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," and preach on grace, faith and scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catholic Church, the Mass at its heart, and one word. Your line was universal. Did you hear what a Catholic friend loves? Day two hundred eighty-nine.

October 31, 1517. Wittenberg, a small university town in Germany. A thirty-three-year-old monk and professor named Martin Luther has written ninety-five short arguments, in Latin, against the sale of indulgences: certificates people bought believing they would shorten the punishment of their dead loved ones after death. A preacher named Tetzel was working the region, and people were paying. The story goes that Luther walked to the door of the castle church and nailed the theses up with a hammer. Historians argue about the hammer. What's certain is that he mailed them to his archbishop that same day. He wanted a debate among scholars. Instead, printers translated them into German and within weeks they were everywhere. He'd started something much bigger than a debate. Today's word is its name.
screen: `WITTENBERG, OCTOBER 31, 1517.` → `NINETY-FIVE THESES.` → `A DEBATE THAT GOT AWAY.`

segments.voice: The Reformation is the name for the movement that began with Luther and reshaped Western Christianity in the 1500s. Reform means to form again, to bring back into shape. Luther didn't set out to start a new church. He wanted to reform the one he belonged to. But under the argument about indulgences lay a question that had tormented him for years. He'd been a desperately serious monk, confessing for hours, never sure he'd done enough to stand before a holy God. Then, reading Paul's letter to the Romans, he fastened on one line, "The just shall live by faith," and he said it felt like the gates of paradise opening. Righteousness wasn't something he had to earn. It was a gift. Ephesians puts it in one sentence: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." From that grew the Reformers' slogans, in Latin: by grace alone, by faith alone, by scripture alone. Luther translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it, and he wrote hymns for whole congregations to sing. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent. Catholics also taught, and teach, that salvation is God's gift of grace, but they understood faith, works and the church's role differently, and the two sides condemned each other. Wars followed, and the West was divided. Five hundred years later, Catholics and Lutherans have found they agree on more than their ancestors thought. We'll come to that later. For today, just the line that set a monk free.
screen: `REFORM: TO FORM AGAIN.` · `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.` · `BY GRACE, FAITH, AND SCRIPTURE ALONE.` · `TRENT ANSWERS; THE WEST DIVIDES.` · then, large: `FOR BY GRACE ARE YE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Ephesians 2:8, slowly, three times. For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. Settle, and breathe. Notice the word gift. Think of something in your life you know you didn't earn: a person, a morning, a second chance. Hold it like a gift, not a wage. If you pray, you can give thanks for grace. If you don't, just rest in the idea that not everything has to be earned. The bell holds the time.
Reformation. The movement, begun by Martin Luther in 1517, to bring the Western church back into shape around grace, faith and scripture.
Your line: by grace, through faith. Today, when you catch yourself trying to earn something that was already given, stop, and just receive it. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

original.note: Greek: grace, a free gift, favor. The word in Ephesians 2:8, and the root of charity and charisma.

trapdoor: what you thought: an angry monk hammered a list on a door and started a new church.
what it means: a movement to re-form the church around grace, faith and scripture, which divided Western Christianity.
